### Strategy Spotlight
Covered-call ETFs such as the Hamilton Enhanced Canadian Covered Call ETF generate monthly income by selling out-of-the-money calls against a basket of Canadian equities. In the current environment of moderating GIC renewal rates, the 9.8 percent indicated yield offers a concrete alternative for income-focused accounts that can tolerate the capped upside and potential drawdowns during equity rallies. Investors can implement the approach directly through a TFSA or RRSP by purchasing HDIV on the TSX and holding for the monthly distribution cycle, or by replicating the mechanics themselves on individual holdings using their broker's options chain. The strategy has historically performed best in range-bound or modestly rising markets where volatility supports premium collection, but it underperforms sharply in strong trending bull markets when the calls are exercised away. Risk management requires monitoring the underlying equity exposure and being prepared to accept assignment or roll the calls if the market moves sharply higher. The ETF pays distributions monthly, which aligns with retiree cash-flow needs that previously relied on five-year GICs now renewing at lower rates. Canadian investors can compare the 9.8 percent yield directly against current GIC quotes and decide whether the equity risk premium justifies the move into covered-call structures. Source: [fool.ca](https://www.fool.ca/2026/10/15/retirees-dont-want-to-wait-a-year-for-that-gic-to-mature-this-9-8-dividend-play-pays-monthly/)
---
### Investor Education: Quarterly Portfolio Review Mechanics
Imagine you hold Enbridge in your TFSA and want to verify whether the recent bought-deal issuance and acquisition spending have shifted your overall allocation targets. The review begins by exporting your account holdings into a spreadsheet and calculating each position's percentage of total portfolio value using current market prices rather than cost basis. Enbridge trades near $66 per share after raising roughly $3 billion in a bought-deal to fund US pipeline and utility acquisitions that now total more than US$3 billion on top of the earlier US$14 billion natural gas utility purchases. Next compare those weights against your stated targets, noting any drift above or below your tolerance bands, then calculate time-weighted returns by isolating each cash flow date and applying the appropriate growth factor. Review realized versus unrealized gains to identify tax-loss harvesting candidates before year-end, and separately track the trailing twelve-month dividend income trend to confirm whether the income stream is stable or eroding. Enbridge has raised its dividend in each of the past 31 years while advancing more than $40 billion in secured capital projects tied to North American energy demand growth from AI data centers and LNG exports. Subtract all fees paid in the quarter from the gross return to isolate the true net performance, then run a simple decision checklist: rebalance only if drift exceeds your band, harvest losses only if the tax benefit exceeds transaction costs, and add new capital only to names that still meet your original thesis criteria. The key misconception to avoid is treating the review as a performance scorecard instead of a rules-based rebalancing and tax-planning exercise.

**Market Pulse:** S&P 500 closed at 7,719 (-1.1%), NASDAQ at 26,693 (-1.9%), and TSX Composite at 35,584 (-1.1%). Sentiment weakened on firm September core CPI at +0.33% MoM and 2.6% YoY alongside Beige Book notes of tariff and energy uncertainty. The Fed's October 27-28 meeting now carries higher stakes after the inflation print, with markets pricing limited room for near-term cuts. Banks and gold miners led the TSX decline while broader rotation pressured growth names. The nearest Bank of Canada decision sits weeks out with rate-sensitive sectors still repricing the path. About 14 days ago we picked BTE.TO on a valuation screen showing resilient cash flow amid commodity volatility and it closed +2.03%, a reminder that contract-protected energy names can buffer short-term swings when volume supports the entry.
---
### Strategy Spotlight
Single-stock ETFs let investors gain targeted exposure to names like Alphabet without buying the underlying shares outright. Today's launch of six PowerStock single-stock ETFs on the TSX, including GOOP tracking Alphabet, gives Canadian investors a new vehicle for concentrated bets inside registered accounts. Implementation starts with checking the ETF's premium or discount to NAV on your platform and sizing the position to match your existing sector limits. These products have historically performed best in low-volatility regimes where single-name momentum persists, but they amplify drawdowns when the underlying rotates. Always compare the ETF's management fee and liquidity against simply holding the stock or a broad sector ETF. The new funds also simplify foreign-exchange handling for U.S. names, removing the need to manage separate currency conversions on each trade. Canadian investors can therefore maintain precise weights in high-conviction names while staying within TFSA contribution limits and avoiding direct custody of U.S. shares. Liquidity and tracking error should be monitored closely in the first weeks of trading to ensure the ETF does not deviate materially from the underlying stock's performance. Source: [kalkinemedia.com](https://kalkinemedia.com/ca/news/announcements/global-x-canada-unveils-six-powerstock-single-stock-etfs-on-tsx-featuring-goop-tracking-alphabet)
---
### Investor Education: Canadian Discount Brokerages Compared
Imagine you want to buy 100 shares of a TSX-listed energy name at the open; Wealthsimple Trade executes commission-free but routes through a single market maker that can widen the spread by 3-5 cents on less-liquid names during the first 15 minutes. Questrade charges $4.95-$9.95 per trade yet offers free ETF purchases and direct access to U.S. exchanges with real-time Level 2 data on its higher tier. Interactive Brokers posts the lowest margin rates at roughly 6.5% for balances under $100k and supports 150+ global markets, though its platform requires learning a steeper interface. Bank-owned brokerages such as TD Direct Investing integrate seamlessly with chequing accounts but levy $9.99 commissions plus higher foreign-exchange spreads on U.S. trades. The pro habit is to run a side-by-side cost calculator for your typical trade size and frequency before committing, then route larger U.S. orders through the lowest-fee desk. The misconception that “free is always cheapest” ignores hidden spreads and limited order types that can cost active investors more than a transparent commission. Canadian investors also need to verify which platforms support automatic dividend reinvestment inside registered accounts, because missing that feature can force manual purchases that incur extra commissions or FX fees. Finally, margin availability and interest rates matter for those who occasionally use leverage; Interactive Brokers' lower rates can save hundreds of dollars annually on a $50,000 borrowed balance compared with bank platforms, but only if the investor is comfortable navigating its order types and reporting tools.
---

Contributing TFSA room early is a simple planning tactic that locks in the full annual limit without waiting for December. Implementation is straightforward on any brokerage platform: transfer the amount from a non-registered account or cash balance as soon as the new room is available on January 1. The approach has worked best in years when contribution-room changes or tax-year deadlines create last-minute rushes. The main risk is opportunity cost if the cash earns higher interest outside the TFSA, but that is usually small relative to the planning certainty gained. ### Investor Education: The Canadian Home Bias Problem
An investor who keeps 40% of a TFSA in TSX-listed financials and energy names because they feel familiar with the companies is effectively doubling down on the same economic exposures already embedded in their job and housing. The mechanism that creates the gap is simple: Canada represents roughly 3% of global equity market capitalization, yet many portfolios hold 30-50% in Canadian stocks, producing heavy concentration in two sectors that together make up about half the TSX. A pro habit that narrows the gap is to run a quick geographic allocation report in the brokerage once a quarter and compare the Canadian weight against the MSCI World ex-Canada benchmark. The common misconception is that familiarity with domestic names automatically justifies the overweight; the fix is to treat home bias as an explicit, sized decision rather than the default.
